definition: Genetic programming (GP) is an evolutionary algorithm, an artificial intelligence technique mimicking natural evolution, which operates on a population of programs.
details: It applies the genetic operators selection according to a predefined fitness measure, mutation and crossover. The crossover operation involves swapping specified parts of selected pairs (parents) to produce new and different offspring that become part of the new generation of programs. Some programs not selected for reproduction are copied from the current generation to the new generation. Mutation involves substitution of some random part of a program with some other random part of a program. Then the selection and other operations are recursively applied to the new generation of programs. Typically, members of each new generation are on average more fit than the members of the previous generation, and the best-of-generation program is often better than the best-of-generation programs from previous generations. Termination of the evolution usually occurs when some individual program reaches a predefined proficiency or fitness level. It may and often does happen that a particular run of the algorithm results in premature convergence to some local maximum that is not a globally optimal or even good solution. explainer.lead: Genetic programming automatically improves a population of computer programs by imitating natural evolution. Instead of writing every rule by hand, you define what a good program should achieve and let selection, mutation, and crossover search for one.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a class where everyone writes a slightly different recipe for solving the same puzzle. The best recipes get to share parts, some parts are changed at random, and a few recipes are kept unchanged; then the new group tries the puzzle again. After many rounds, one recipe may solve it well enough.
tiers.practitioner: To apply GP, define a program representation, a fitness function, and rules for selection, crossover, and mutation, then iterate until a fitness target is met. A run can converge prematurely to a poor local maximum, so strong results should not be assumed from one run; dozens to hundreds of runs are usually necessary for a very good solution.
tiers.paperLevel: GP evolves a population P_t of programs using fitness-based selection S, crossover C, and mutation M, with some unselected programs copied unchanged: P_(t+1) is formed from S(P_t), C, M, and copying. Fitness determines reproductive success, and termination normally occurs when an individual reaches a predefined fitness level. Average and best-of-generation fitness often improve, but neither global optimality nor monotonic improvement is guaranteed, and runs may converge to local maxima.

explainer.example: Suppose the task is to find an arithmetic program that outputs x + 1, with fitness based on how few test cases it gets wrong. If the population contains x + 2, a mutation replacing 2 with 1 produces x + 1; that program passes every test, reaches the target fitness, and ends the run.
explainer.goal: Evolve a program that performs well according to a predefined fitness measure, stopping when one reaches the required level.
outputs: A new generation of programs after each evolutionary cycle
A program that reaches the target fitness, if the run succeeds
steps: Start with a population of programs.
Select parent programs according to fitness.
Swap specified parts of selected parents through crossover.
Replace random program parts through mutation, and copy some unselected programs unchanged.
Evaluate the new generation and repeat until a program reaches the target fitness.
tradeoffs: Searches programs automatically once fitness and genetic operations are defined
Often produces fitter generations and better best-of-generation programs
Can converge prematurely to a local maximum that is not a good solution
Usually requires dozens to hundreds of runs to obtain a very good solution
